newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices up, conditions good.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices up, conditions good.

text.p: Australian grains ended a busy week last Friday with prices up but opinions divided on whether they were on the verge of a bull run.
Australian wheat shipments also continued to run high at 515,626 million tonnes for the week, up from 229,037 tonnes the week before.
This brought shipments to 8.92 million tonnes for the shipping year so far, well up from 6.06 million in the previous corresponding period, as Australia chases wheat export records.
Interest returned to both cash and futures markets for wheat over the week, with the two markets feeding off each other.
Futures prices rose well on Tuesday in reaction to tight world feed grain markets and advancing prices, fuelling further strength in cash markets.
Australian Wheat Board quoted prices for 1996/97 crop wheat remained steady over the week but indicator prices for new crop wheat rose by A$1.00 a tonne to A$146.50 Newcastle.
Traders agreed markets were turning up but saw prospects and cash grain movements differently over the week.
"It's been a busy week," Guy Allen of GrainCorp said.

Allen saw the cash market mostly steady over the week, in moderate trading, with Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat ending on A$172.00-A$174.00 delivered Newcastle, with deferred months trading a couple of dollars higher.

Bill Mitchell at New England Agricultural Traders, based in the New South Wales country centre of Armidale, saw ASW cash prices rising by about A$10.00 a tonne to trade at A$186.00 a tonne Newcastle at one stage during the week.
"(The market) is wanting to turn up," Allen said. "The thing that's keeping it down is the stronger (Australian) dollar."
"It's keeping people a bit pessimistic but we're starting to see some end user demand as well as producers coming to town to sell some grain. Activity's picked up a bit."
The tone of the next few weeks would be determined by the northern hemisphere weather and spring wheat plantings, he said.
Soybeans had already produced some excitement with a strong rise during the week before falling back, he pointed out.
Mitchell said domestic cash wheat was squeezed during the week, with some supplies available but growers holding it for tax reasons until the new financial year, which begins July 1.
Mitchell does not see the market rising strongly.
"I think we're looking to trade toward the top side of an expanded range, but I don't believe we're entering into a bull market," he said.
Both Allen and Mitchell saw cash sorghum rising by AS3.00-A$4.00 over the week to A$160.00-A$162.00 Newcastle, as harvest activity began.
On new crops, significant increases in Australia's canola plantings were expected and attention was turning to wheat plantings, Allen said.
"We're going into planting season with good moisture profiles and a very good anticipated start to next year," he said. This was seen keeping a cap on the market.

Over the week, the nearby March 1997 wheat futures contract rose by A$2.50 to A$180.00 a tonne on settlement prices, May 1997 rose by A$5.00 to A$181.50 while September 1997 rose by A$8.00 to A$181.50. The most distant contract, July 1988, rose by A$2.00 to A$172.50.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
